speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
subtopic: THE LATE PRIME MINISTER BARROW OF BARBADOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like very briefly to indicate to the House my very deep personal sorrow and that of my wife at the passing of Prime Minister Barrow on the Island nation of Barbados. May I take this opportunity to join with you, Sir, and the Speaker of the Senate in extending our own family's deepest condolences to the family of the late Prime Minister Barrow.
May I say to my colleagues that Prime Minister Barrow was a great Commonwealth parliamentarian, a great Caribbeanist, a great strength for the eastern Caribbean states, and a great source of strength to democracy in that part of the world. The loss of his presence will be deeply regretted by those who pursue democracy, by those who have a compassion for their people, and by those who look to the Caribbean as it grows and strengthens. .
Many will recall that Prime Minister Barrow was the father of confederation of the eastern Caribbean states, although it did not live in the sense that our Confederation lives and, indeed, is reborn today. Nevertheless, the path that he carved out for those island nations will be long remembered and cherished by all of those who were there and by all of those of Caribbean descent, particularly those of Barbadian descent here in the great country of Canada.

subsubtopic: CORRECTIONAL SERVICE CANADA-SUPPORT FOR EARLY RETIREMENT OPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, air traffic controllers, members of the Armed Forces and RCMP officers are all entitled to take early retirement. I think this is an entirely appropriate recognition of the demanding nature of their jobs and the importance of the services they provide. But I remind the House of another group of workers who perform an equally dangerous, stressful and important job and who do not now have the option of early retirement.
I refer of course to the employees of Correctional Service Canada about whom there seems to be a consensus in this House that they ought to have the opportunity for early retirement pursuant to the unanimous recommendations of the Sub-Committee on Penitentiaries 10 years ago. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) has written to the National President of the Union of Solicitor General Employees promising his support for the early retirement option. I know a number of my colleagues on this side of the House have indicated their support and have urged the Government to act.
Frankly, I do not understand the problem. There is substantial agreement in the House that Correctional Service employees deserve to have the option of early retirement open to them. This question is one which could be dealt with quickly and easily. The ball is now in the Government's court. I urge the Government to introduce the appropriate legislation as quickly as possible.
Canada's correctional workers have waited long enough.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY TO PROTECT WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians enjoy some of the most beautiful lakes and rivers in the world. With less than 1 per cent of the world's population Canada contains as much as 25 per cent of the global supply of fresh water.
All of us derive benefit from Canada's abundance of water assets. During Environment Week we should be especially mindful of the need for adequate protection of these resources.
In the past we were as a people not as vigilant as we should have been concerning the pollution of our waterways. But we

June 3, 1987
can look ahead for a better future if we ensure sound water management.
Much has been done already. At the federal level, agreements with the United States are contributing to protection against the ravages of industrial pollution. In many of our communities, urban and rural, programs have been enacted in recent years to undo the damage caused and to clean some of our lakes, rivers and canals.
We must do more. It is up to all of us.

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF PROVISIONS OF BILL C-55
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent public opinion polls on refugee policy show that Canadians are maintaining their traditional open-mindedness.
Most believe that Canada should continue to accept refugees in numbers appropriate to our ability to assist them to establish themselves and their families in our country.
Polls also indicate that Canadians want the Government to deal with the problems created by the backlog in our outmoded refugee determination process. But is the Government's Bill C-55 the right response? The Bill proposes pre-selection at our borders, a system which some suspect as being aimed more at finding reasons to send refugees elsewhere than at assessing the legitimacy of refugee claims.
The Bill proposes establishing a list of so-called safe countries for this purpose, but it does not explain on what criteria the list is to be set up, how quickly it can be revised in response to changing world events, or how the Government can guarantee safety in another country.
Clearing the backlog will, in itself, discourage abuse of Canada's refugee determination process and make it easier to serve and assist genuine refugees. Canadians, who were the proud recipients of the United Nations Nansen Medal for their enlightened approach to the world refugee crisis, must think twice about Bill C-55.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL CONFERENCE OF FEDERATION OF CANADIAN MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Sunday last delegates from across Canada began arriving in Ottawa to attend the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Fiftieth Annual Conference which ends today.
Over 900 delegates representing 402 municipalities are attending the conference celebrating the theme "A golden past and a brilliant future". They have come from as far away and as diverse places as the District of West Vancouver in the West, St. John's in the East, and, of course, Swift Current, Saskatchewan.
The delegates are addressing important municipal issues, ranging from liability insurance to water infrastructure, to privatization in municipal government.
We congratulate these delegates on their commitment to their communities and their country. They and their predecessors have travelled to similar conferences over the past 50 years to discuss municipal issues, initiate ideas and to build on those ideas. These are the people who have led Canadian municipalities to a golden past. We welcome them to Ottawa and encourage them in building a brilliant future.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF SPORT FISHING CORRIDOR IN RIVERS INLET AREA OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to call the attention of the House to a serious matter. It is the creation of an exclusive sport fishing corridor in the Rivers Inlet area, a previous commercial fishing area.
This action was unilaterally taken by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, contrary to the recommendation of the Central Coast Advisory Board.
This sets a dangerous precedent and process under way, where one or two local individuals can override the wishes of the majority of the community and the established advisory boards. I call on the Minister to revoke the sport fishing corridor in the Rivers Inlet area and request the Central Coast Advisory Board, with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, to work out an acceptable fishing plan for the area.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO RIGHT HON. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
In 1534, Mr. Speaker, European explorator Jacques Cartier left Saint-Malo in France and sailed across the Atlantic on his way to become the storied discoverer of Canada. Soon after, French Europeans settlers were joined by English Europeans. It took only a few centuries for the descendants of these two great peoples to cross the whole Canadian continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific to create a huge new country whose population swelled with the arrival of many nationals from other countries.
June 3, 1987

In 1867 the Fathers of Confederation gathered in Charlottetown to witness a major constitutional event. Thanks to the good will of all regions of Canada their agreement prevailed until 1982, but the 1982 agreement turned out to be incomplete.
Today, June 3, 1987, ten Provincial Premiers representing four different political Parties have agreed on a historic definition of Canada. It is a consensus with history, with geography, with the economy, with our cultures, and with our various ethnic communities. Today, Mr. Speaker, we pay tribute to the architect of this event, to Canada's statesman, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S PARTICIPATION-CONGRATULATIONS TO ARCHITECTS OF ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Quebecers and Canadians I think we can rejoice in the constitutional accord which paved the way for Quebec's endorsing of the Canadian Constitution last evening or this morning.
And like everyone else, I should think, I extend my congratulations to the Premier of Quebec, the Hon. Robert Bourassa, and to Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Remil-lard who, since the 1985 elections, has been criss-crossing the country in an attempt to convince the other Provincial Premiers that Quebec should be urged to join the Constitution.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I also congratulate the Provincial Premiers who at last have come to appreciate the Canadian reality.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S PARTICIPATION-CONGRATULATIONS TO ARCHITECTS OF ACCORD
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S PARTICIPATION-CONGRATULATIONS TO ARCHITECTS OF ACCORD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also want to congratulate the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) for being the first leader in Canada to demonstrate open-mindedness with respect to Quebec's participation in the Canadian Constitution.

subsubtopic: SIGNIFICANCE OF CONSTITUTIONAL ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the most important amendment since the patriation of our Constitution was signed.
Mr. Speaker, in concrete terms this means that Quebec has returned to the Canadian constitutional fold and that our Government has kept its promise to make Canada a united country, where the rights of English-speaking and Frenchspeaking Canadians are respected.
For Quebec, it means that the province will be able to select and receive its own immigrants; to propose nominations for senators from Quebec; to propose nominations for the three judges representing one third of the Supreme Court; and to promote and protect the French character of that province, in addition to obtaining a non-derogation clause with respect to language rights.
Mr. Speaker, for the first time in our history, the right to financial compensation for opting out has been enshrined in the Constitution. A great victory for the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, today is a great day. It is the first day of a united and strong Canada, open to all and attuned to the needs of Canadians. A unique Canada in the image of its Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Mr. Speaker, no more confrontation and arrogance. Make way for positive action and a modern, united and generous Canada.

subtopic: CHALLENGE '87 SEED PROGRAM-CATHOLIC YOUTH ORGANIZATION'S APPLICATION DENIED
CHALLENGE '87 SEED PROGRAM-CATHOLIC YOUTH ORGANIZATION'S APPLICATION DENIED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am outraged to learn that the application of the Catholic Youth Organization to the Challenge '87 SEED program has been denied.
The CYO depends upon student summer employment programs to provide one-on-one programs for exceptional children whose disability prevents them from taking part in regular camping activities. This is the only summer outlet for exceptional children, particularly those with social and emotional disabilities and severe learning problems.
More than 100 disabled children will miss out on summer camp this year because of the Mulroney Government's decision to cut off funding to the CYO.
Indeed it is truly a sad day for Canada when the Conservative Government wants to reduce the deficit on the backs of disabled children. How quickly Rick Hansen's struggle is forgotten.

June 3, 1987

subsubtopic: EXTRAORDINARY WORK ACCOMPLISHED BY PRIME MINISTER AND PROVINCIAL COUNTERPARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was and I am proud to be a Canadian, and from now on I will be even prouder.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Premiers of the provinces have put in long hours of hard work to reach a consensus representing the various interests and cultures of this beautiful country of ours.

The naysayers, those "quick-blooming" critics of the last few days, were determined to undermine the political will for national reconciliation so strongly expressed in the last election. They even contradicted themselves.
However, in recognizing our differences and confirming our constitutional right to be different, this agreement to unite Canadians truly represents a superb best effort on the part of the Leaders of our Governments and particularly our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister indicated that consultations and discussions would continue. In any case, as an English-speaking Canadian and a Quebecer, 1 would like to thank our leaders for their exceptional work, and I think we should all celebrate their outstanding success.

subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONAL ACCORD-NEGOTIATING TALENTS AND LEADERSHIP OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as of today we can say that we have a real Canada, united, dynamic, stronger than ever thanks to the efforts of our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, who showed exceptional political know-how and a deep commitment to put an end to Quebec's constitutional isolation.
The Prime Minister and the ten Premiers, especially Quebec's Premier, Mr. Robert Bourassa, turned a page in this country's history, and Quebec's enthusiastic and honourable entry into the Constitution marks the beginning of a chapter that will allow us to build a new Canada for the coming decades. This Conservative Government proved capable of reaching an accord with ten provincial Governments representing four different parties, thereby meeting with courage, stamina and persistence the challenge of national reconciliation. This points to the negotiating and leadership abilities of our Prime Minister, who turned into a constitutional agreement the understanding in principle reached at Meech Lake.
Mr. Speaker, I feel great satisfaction today at being a Canadian and a Quebecer, and with the support of my constituents in Chambly, may I tell you, Mr. Prime Minister-
I want to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for giving Canadians not two but one Canada.
